title: Animals in groups: a school of fish
subject: Life science

steps.title: School of fish
steps.instruction: Trace every small fish in the group.

note.text: Many small fish swim close together in a group called a school. They turn and move as one.

steps.title: Predator
steps.instruction: Trace the big fish hunting them.

note.text: A predator hunts other animals for food. A big fish like a tuna hunts small fish.

steps.title: Eye and mouth
steps.instruction: Draw the predator's eye and mouth.

note.text: A predator needs to pick out one fish to catch, but a swirling school makes that hard.

steps.title: Escape
steps.instruction: Draw the arrows showing the school splitting to escape.

note.text: Many eyes spot danger sooner, and the group splits and swirls to confuse the predator.
note.remember: Groups help animals find food, defend themselves and survive.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: How does swimming in a school help small fish survive?

options.text: It's harder for a predator to pick out and catch one fish
options.feedback: Yes. Many moving fish confuse the predator, and many eyes spot it sooner.

options.text: The school can fight off the big fish
options.feedback: Small fish can't fight a tuna. They escape by confusing it.

options.text: Fish in a school don't need food
options.feedback: They still need food. Groups can even help them find it.

options.text: It makes the fish grow bigger
options.feedback: Groups help with safety and finding food, not size.

steps.title: Other groups
steps.question: Which of these is another animal group that helps its members survive?

options.feedback: Yes. Wolves cooperate to catch animals much bigger than one wolf could.

options.text: A single bear sleeping in a cave
options.feedback: That's one animal alone. Look for animals working together.

options.text: A spider alone in its web
options.feedback: Most spiders hunt alone. A group means animals working together.
A rock isn't alive. Look for animals in a group.
